source_text: Οὕτω καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἐποίησε, καθάπερ ἐν καλιᾷ, τῇ Παλαιστίνῃ τρέφων τοὺς μαθητάς· ἐπειδὴ δὲ πέτεσθαι ἐδίδαξε παρὼν καὶ διαβαστάζων αὐτοὺς, τέλος ἀφῆκεν εἰς τὴν οἰκουμένην πτῆναι, κελεύσας καὶ ἑαυτοῖς πολλαχοῦ βοηθεῖν. Καὶ ὅτι τοῦτό ἐστιν ἀληθὲς, καὶ ἵνα τὴν δύναμιν αὐτοῦ μάθωσι, πάντων αὐτοὺς ἐγύμνωσε, καὶ μονοχίτωνας ἀπέστειλε, καὶ χωρὶς ὑποδημάτων ἐκέλευσε βαδίζειν, αὐτῆς οὖν τῆς ῥήσεως ἀκούσαντες σαφῶς εἰσόμεθα. Οὐ γὰρ ἁπλῶς εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Ἄρατε βαλάντιον καὶ πήραν, ἀλλ' ἀνέμνησεν αὐτοὺς τῶν προτέρων, οὕτως εἰπών· Ὅτε ἀπέστειλα ὑμᾶς ἄτερ βαλαντίου καὶ πήρας, μή τινος ὑστερήσατε; τουτέστιν, Οὐ πάντα μετὰ ἀφθονίας ὑμῖν ἐπέῤῥει, καὶ πολλῆς ἀπελαύσατε δαψιλείας; ἀλλὰ νῦν βούλομαι ὑμᾶς καὶ δι' ἑαυτῶν ἀγωνίζεσθαι· βούλομαι ὑμᾶς καὶ πενίας πεῖραν λαβεῖν· διὰ τοῦτο λοιπὸν ἐπὶ τὴν ἀνάγκην οὐκ ἄγω τοῦ προτέρου νόμου, ἀλλ' ἐπιτρέπω καὶ βαλάντιον ἔχειν καὶ πήραν, ἵνα μὴ, καθάπερ δι' ἀψύχων ὀργάνων, ἐνεργεῖν τὰ καθ' ὑμᾶς νομίζωμαι, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὑμεῖς τὴν οἰκείαν ἔχητε ἐπιδείκνυσθαι φιλοσοφίαν. γʹ. Καὶ τί, φησὶν, οὐκ ἂν μείζων ἐφάνη ἡ χάρις, εἰ διαπαντὸς οὕτως ἐτέλεσαν ὄντες; Ἀλλ' αὐτοὶ οὐκ ἐγένοντο οὕτω δόκιμοι· εἰ γὰρ μηδεμιᾶς ἔλαβον θλίψεως πεῖραν, μὴ πενίας, μὴ διωγμοῦ, μὴ στενοχωρίας, ἔμειναν ἂν ἀργοὶ καὶ νωθεῖς· νῦν δὲ οὐχὶ τὴν χάριν διαλάμψαι μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν τῶν ὑπακουόντων δοκιμὴν ἠθέλησεν ἐπιδειχθῆναι, ἵνα μὴ μετὰ ταῦτά τινες ἔχωσι λέγειν, ὅτι Οὐδὲν παρ' ἑαυτῶν εἰσήνεγκαν ἐκεῖνοι, ἀλλὰ τὸ πᾶν τῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ ῥοπῆς ἐγένετο. Ἠδύνατο μὲν γὰρ αὐτοὺς ὁ Θεὸς μέχρι τέλους ἐν ἀφθονίᾳ καταστῆσαι τοσαύτῃ, ἀλλ' οὐκ ἠθέλησε διὰ πολλὰς καὶ ἀναγκαίας προφάσεις, ἃς πολλάκις πρὸς τὴν ὑμετέραν ἀγάπην εἰρήκαμεν· μίαν μὲν δὴ ταύτην, ἑτέραν δὲ οὐκ ἐλάττονα ταύτης, ἵνα καὶ μετριάζειν εἰδῶσι· τρίτην δὲ, ἵνα μὴ μείζονα ἢ κατὰ ἄνθρωπον λάβωσι δόξαν. Διὰ δὴ ταῦτα, καὶ πολλῷ πλείονα τούτων, ἀφεὶς αὐτοὺς πολλοῖς τῶν ἀδοκήτων περιπίπτειν, οὐκ ἠβουλήθη ὑπὸ τὴν ἀκρίβειαν τῆς νομοθεσίας τῆς προτέρας ἀφεῖναι, ἀλλ' ἐχάλασε καὶ ἀνῆκε τῆς φιλοσοφίας τὸν τόνον ἐκείνης, ὥστε μὴ βαρύν τινα καὶ ἀφόρητον αὐτοῖς γενέσθαι τὸν βίον, πολλαχοῦ ἐγκαταλιμπανομένοις, καὶ τὸν ἀκριβῆ νόμον ἐκεῖνον ἀναγκαζομένοις τηρεῖν. Ἐπειδὴ δὲ χρὴ καὶ τὸ προκείμενον ἀσαφὲς ὂν ποιῆσαι καταφανὲς, ἀναγκαῖον καὶ τοῦτο εἰπεῖν. Εἰπὼν γὰρ, Ὁ ἔχων βαλάντιον, ἀράτω, καὶ πήραν, ἐπήγαγε· Καὶ ὁ μὴ ἔχων, πωλήσει τὸ ἱμάτιον αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἀγοράσει μάχαιραν. Τί ποτε τοῦτό ἐστι; καθοπλίζει τοὺς μαθητὰς ὁ λέγων, Ἐάν τίς σε ῥαπίσῃ εἰς τὴν δεξιὰν σιαγόνα, στρέψον αὐτῷ καὶ τὴν ἄλλην; ὁ κελεύων εὐλογεῖν τοὺς λοιδορουμένους, ἀνέχεσθαι τῶν ἐπηρεαζόντων, εὔχεσθαι ὑπὲρ τῶν διωκόντων, εἶτα καθοπλίζει, καὶ διὰ μαχαίρας μόνης; Καὶ ποῖον ἂν ἔχοι τοῦτο λόγον; Εἰ γὰρ ὅλως ἔδει καθοπλίσαι, οὐ μαχαίρας ἔδει κτήσασθαι μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀσπίδα καὶ κράνος καὶ κνημῖδας. Ὅλως δὲ, εἴ γε ἀνθρωπίνως τὰ τοιαῦτα ἔμελλεν οἰκονομεῖν, πόσοις οὐκ ἦν τὸ ἐπίταγμα γέλως; Εἰ γὰρ μυρία τοιαῦτα ὅπλα ἐκτήσαντο πρὸς τοσαύτην ἔφοδον καὶ ἐπιβουλὴν δήμων, τυράννων, πόλεων, ἐθνῶν, τίνες ἔμελλον οἱ ἕνδεκα φανεῖσθαι; Φωνῆς γὰρ ἀκοῦσαι χρεμετίζοντος ἵππου δυνατὸν ἦν αὐτοῖς; πρὸς δὲ τὴν ὄψιν μόνην οὐκ ἂν κατεπλάγησαν τῶν στρατοπέδων, ἐν λίμναις καὶ ποταμοῖς καὶ ἀκατίοις τραφέντες μικροῖς; Τίνος οὖν ἕνεκεν τοῦτο λέγει; Τὴν ἔφοδον τῶν Ἰουδαίων ἐνδείξασθαι βουλόμενος, καὶ ὅτι μέλλουσιν αὐτὸν συλλαμβάνειν.
thought_title: Christ trains the disciples like birds, then explains the sword saying
orientation: Chrysostom is explaining why Christ first sent the disciples with nothing and later told them to take purse, bag, and sword, using the image of a bird teaching its young to fly.
pass_a_gloss: In this way also Christ acted, just as in a nest, in Palestine nourishing the disciples; but when he had taught them to fly, being present and carrying them, at last he let them fly into the inhabited world, commanding them also in many places to help themselves. And that this is true, and in order that they might learn his power, he stripped them of all things, and sent them with one garment, and commanded them to walk without sandals; therefore having heard the very saying we shall know clearly. For he did not simply say to them: Take a purse and a bag, but he reminded them of the former things, saying thus: When I sent you without purse and bag, did you lack anything? that is, Did not all things flow to you with abundance, and did you not enjoy great plenty? but now I wish you also to strive through yourselves; I wish you also to receive experience of poverty; for this reason henceforth I do not lead you to the necessity of the former law, but I permit you to have both purse and bag, in order that I may not be thought to work the things concerning you as through lifeless instruments, but that you also may have your own discipline to display. 3. And why, he says, would not the grace have appeared greater, if they had continued being thus throughout? But they themselves did not become so approved; for if they had received experience of no affliction, not of poverty, not of persecution, not of distress, they would have remained idle and sluggish; but now he wished not only the grace to shine forth, but also the approvedness of those who obey to be displayed, in order that after these things some might not be able to say, that Those men contributed nothing from themselves, but the whole thing was of God's inclination. For God was able to establish them until the end in such great abundance, but he did not wish it for many and necessary reasons, which we have often spoken to your love; one indeed this, and another not less than this, in order that they might know also to be moderate; and a third, in order that they might not receive glory greater than according to man. For indeed for these reasons, and for many more than these, allowing them to fall into many unexpected things, he did not wish to leave them under the strictness of the former legislation, but he relaxed and loosened the tension of that discipline, so that their life might not become heavy and unbearable for them, being left behind in many places and being compelled to keep that strict law. But since it is necessary also to make the matter before us, being unclear, manifest, it is necessary also to say this. For having said, He who has a purse, let him take it, and a bag, he added: And he who does not have, let him sell his garment, and buy a sword. What ever is this? he arms the disciples, he who says, If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn to him also the other? he who commands to bless those who revile, to endure those who insult, to pray for those who persecute, then he arms them, and with a sword only? And what reason would this have? For if it was necessary at all to arm them, it was necessary to acquire not a sword only, but also a shield and a helmet and greaves. And in general, if he was going to manage such things in a human way, to how many would the command not be a laughingstock? For if they had acquired ten thousand such weapons against so great an attack and plot of peoples, tyrants, cities, nations, what were the eleven going to appear to be? For was it possible for them to hear the voice of a neighing horse? would they not have been terrified at the mere sight of the armies, having been raised among lakes and rivers and small boats? For what reason then does he say this? Wishing to indicate the attack of the Jews, and that they are about to seize him.

pass_b_english: Christ did the same. He nourished the disciples in Palestine as in a nest, and when he had taught them to fly by being present and carrying them along, he finally let them fly out into the world, commanding them in many places to help themselves. That this is true, and that they might learn his power, he stripped them of everything, sent them with one garment, and commanded them to walk without sandals. We will know this clearly when we hear the very words. For he did not simply say to them, “Take a purse and a bag,” but he reminded them of what had gone before, saying, “When I sent you out without a purse or a bag, did you lack anything?” (Luke 22:35). That is, “Did not everything flow to you with abundance, and did you not enjoy great plenty? But now I want you to strive on your own. I want you to gain experience of poverty. For this reason I no longer hold you to the necessity of the former rule, but I permit you to have a purse and a bag, so that I may not be thought to work out your affairs through lifeless instruments, but you also may have your own discipline to display.”

But someone might say, “Would not the grace have appeared greater if they had remained that way to the end?” But they themselves were not yet so approved. For if they had gained no experience of affliction, no poverty, no persecution, no distress, they would have remained idle and sluggish. Now he wanted not only the grace to shine forth, but also the approvedness of those who obeyed to be displayed, so that afterward no one could say, “They contributed nothing of their own; everything came from God’s intervention.” God could have kept them in such abundance to the end, but he did not wish to, for many necessary reasons that we have often spoken of to your love. One reason is this; another, no less than this, is that they might learn to be moderate; a third, that they might not receive a glory greater than human. For these reasons, and many more than these, he allowed them to fall into many unexpected things, and he did not wish to leave them under the strictness of the former legislation, but he relaxed and loosened the tension of that discipline, so that their life might not become heavy and unbearable for them, if they were often left on their own and compelled to keep that strict rule.

Since it is necessary to make clear what is obscure in the passage before us, I must speak of this too. For after saying, “Let the one who has a purse take it, and a bag,” he added, “And the one who has no sword, let him sell his cloak and buy one” (Luke 22:36). What can this mean? Does he arm the disciples—he who says, “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also” (Matthew 5:39)? He who commands us to bless those who revile us, to endure those who mistreat us, to pray for those who persecute us—does he then arm them, and with a sword alone? What sense could this have? For if it was necessary to arm them at all, it was necessary to acquire not only a sword, but also a shield and a helmet and greaves. And in any case, if he was going to manage such things in a human way, how many would not have laughed at the command? For if they had acquired ten thousand such weapons against so great an assault and plot of peoples, tyrants, cities, nations, what would the eleven have appeared to be? Could they even have heard the sound of a horse neighing? Would they not have been terrified at the mere sight of armies—they who had been raised among lakes and rivers and little boats? Why then does he say this? He wants to show the assault of the Jews, and that they are about to seize him.

last_rejected.quote: "And the one who has no sword, let him sell his cloak and buy one" (Luke 22:36)
last_rejected.source_quote: Καὶ ὁ μὴ ἔχων, πωλήσει τὸ ἱμάτιον αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἀγοράσει μάχαιραν
last_rejected.why: Source says 'the one who has not' (i.e., a sword), not 'the one who has no sword'. The subject is implied from context.
last_rejected.fix: "And let the one who does not have one sell his cloak and buy a sword" (Luke 22:36)
last_rejected.ruling: μὴ ἔχων with μάχαιραν implied from context is normal Greek idiom; 'no sword' captures the meaning accurately.

last_rejected.quote: to bless those who revile us, to endure those who mistreat us, to pray for those who persecute us
last_rejected.source_quote: εὐλογεῖν τοὺς λοιδορουμένους, ἀνέχεσθαι τῶν ἐπηρεαζόντων, εὔχεσθαι ὑπὲρ τῶν διωκόντων
last_rejected.why: English adds "us" three times, making these first-person commands, but Greek has participles/infinitives without "us"—"to bless those who revile," "to endure those who mistreat," "to pray for those who persecute." The "us" is added, changing the grammatical object and making it personal application rather than general command.
last_rejected.fix: to bless those who revile, to endure those who mistreat, to pray for those who persecute
last_rejected.ruling: Adding 'us' is standard English idiom for general commands; no meaning changed. λοιδορουμένους etc. are naturally rendered with 'us'.

last_rejected.quote: he finally let them fly out into the world
last_rejected.source_quote: τέλος ἀφῆκεν εἰς τὴν οἰκουμένην πτῆναι
last_rejected.why: The Greek says "he let them fly into the world" but the English adds "out"—"fly out into the world." This is natural but adds a direction not explicit. However, πτῆναι with ἀφῆκεν implies release. Not a serious error. Actually the main issue: the English omits the key word "finally" or "at last"—wait, no, "finally" is there. Let me re-check... The English has "finally let them fly out into the world"—"finally" renders τέλος. "out" is added. Minor addition.
last_rejected.fix: he finally let them fly into the world
last_rejected.ruling: 'fly out' naturally renders ἀφῆκεν πτῆναι; 'out' is idiomatic, not a meaning change.

problems.quote: But they themselves were not yet so approved.
problems.source_quote: Ἀλλ' αὐτοὶ οὐκ ἐγένοντο οὕτω δόκιμοι·
problems.why: Turns a counterfactual ('would not have become so proven') into a past fact and adds 'yet,' breaking the logic of the following 'For if...' clause.
problems.fix: But they themselves would not have become so proven.
problems.ruling: οὐκ ἐγένοντο οὕτω δόκιμοι is ‘did not become’; ‘not yet … approved’ adds time and breaks εἰ μηδεμιᾶς … ἔλαβον counterfactual logic.

problems.quote: since they were often left behind and compelled to keep that strict rule.
problems.source_quote: πολλαχοῦ ἐγκαταλιμπανομένοις, καὶ τὸν ἀκριβῆ νόμον ἐκεῖνον ἀναγκαζομένοις τηρεῖν.
problems.why: The participles are conditional ('if'), not causal ('since'); saying they were compelled to keep the strict rule contradicts the previous clause. Also 'left behind' misrenders 'left on their own.'
problems.fix: if they were often left on their own and compelled to keep that strict rule.
problems.ruling: Dative participles ἐγκαταλιμπανομένοις/ἀναγκαζομένοις are hypothetical circumstance with ἵνα μὴ βαρύν, not causal ‘since’; ‘compelled’ fights ἐχάλασε relaxation.

edits.old: since they were often left behind and compelled to keep that strict rule.
edits.new: if they were often left on their own and compelled to keep that strict rule.

fixed: modality ('were not yet so approved'): no edit – οὐκ ἐγένοντο is aorist indicative with no ἄν, a past fact as in the gloss 'did not become so approved', not a counterfactual; 'yet' only makes that past state explicit and fits the following 'For if...' explanation.

modality ('since they were often left behind...'): fixed to conditional 'if' and 'left on their own' for πολλαχοῦ ἐγκαταλιμπανομένοις ... ἀναγκαζομένοις, the hypothetical avoided by relaxing the rule.

problems.source_quote: τὸ πᾶν τῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ ῥοπῆς ἐγένετο.
problems.why: In Chrysostom, ῥοπή means God's active impulse, sway, or intervention (tipping the scale), not mere 'inclination' (preference or tendency).
problems.ruling: ῥοπῆς is divine sway/impetus tipping outcomes, not weak English 'inclination' as preference.

fixed: Fixed inclination -> intervention for τῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ ῥοπῆς: Greek means God's decisive sway/tipping weight, not mere disposition.

last_rejected.quote: That this is true, and that they might learn his power, he stripped them of everything, sent them with one garment, and commanded them to walk without sandals. We will know this clearly when we hear the very words.
last_rejected.source_quote: Καὶ ὅτι τοῦτό ἐστιν ἀληθὲς, καὶ ἵνα τὴν δύναμιν αὐτοῦ μάθωσι, πάντων αὐτοὺς ἐγύμνωσε, καὶ μονοχίτωνας ἀπέστειλε, καὶ χωρὶς ὑποδημάτων ἐκέλευσε βαδίζειν, αὐτῆς οὖν τῆς ῥήσεως ἀκούσαντες σαφῶς εἰσόμεθα.
last_rejected.why: Splitting the Greek sentence leaves 'That this is true' stranded without a main verb, confusingly joined to the purpose clause 'that they might learn his power.'
last_rejected.fix: We will clearly know that this is true—and that he stripped them of everything, sent them with one garment, and commanded them to walk without sandals so they might learn his power—when we hear the very words.
last_rejected.ruling: Greek καὶ ὅτι…ἵνα… both modify ἐγύμνωσε; English attaches them to 'he stripped'—same logic, awkward not major.

last_rejected.quote: But they themselves were not yet so approved.
last_rejected.source_quote: Ἀλλ' αὐτοὶ οὐκ ἐγένοντο οὕτω δόκιμοι·
last_rejected.why: Turns a counterfactual reply to the objector ('would not have become') into a factual past statement and adds 'yet,' which is absent from the Greek.
last_rejected.fix: But they themselves would not have become so approved.
last_rejected.ruling: Greek οὐκ ἐγένοντο is indicative past, not counterfactual; 'yet' adds nuance but meaning matches δόκιμοι.
